en: The *Vajraprabhā-vātavarṣa-śamana-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of South India during the Tang Dynasty.
Thus have I heard. At one time, the Bhagavat was surrounded by his great assembly before and behind him.
While traveling through the kingdom of Magadha,
he encountered a massive black cloud along the road;
it was thick and heavy, accompanied by a swirling, violent wind.
Amidst thunder, lightning, and a sudden downpour of hail and rain,
he spoke to the Venerable Ānanda:
"You should take a new, clean jar."
With the mantra for filling [the vessel] with water,
one subdues and drives away such as the Naga King Vaśuki and all other venomous nagas who afflict the world.
Those who cause calamities by destroying crops, flowers, fruits,
and seeds should all be captured and driven into a jar;
thus shall this wind, cloud, rain, hail, and thunderbolt be stilled.
Then, restrain it.
You shall receive such mantra-dharmas and so forth;
perform the treatment according to the ritual rules.
At that time, the Tathāgata spoke and revealed the mantra for stopping rain in the eastern direction,
saying: *Tadyathā | ku ku ku ku | pramiṣe saṃjinī | pūṣmāyane śi | nayanatami miṃj*.
6. *Cche* (pronounced with a *k’* sound) *paṃca svāhā*.

*Tadyathā | karoma karoma | karoma karoma | saṃkaroma saṃkaroma | saṃkarama saṃkarama | bhuvanagrarāja | āsecamiṇe | svāhā*.

*Eṣaṇa-vinivāraṇa-buddhasatyan tiṣṭha saṃrudha māhāra svāhā.* At that time, the Tathāgata,
having spoken this mantra, [remained silent].
He addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"You should first prepare two *maṇḍalas*, each measuring two cubits,
by cleanly smearing them with plaster before the Buddha and upon the open ground along the road."
First, place a water jar upon the altar before the Buddha.
Holding a willow branch,
insert it into the water jar.
Recite this mantra with a vigorous and rapid voice while stirring the water in a circular motion; thereby,
one shall capture the Naga King Vasuki and all other venomous nagas.
Place them all inside a water jar.
Twenty-one times, one should use the water from the jar to moisten the ground within the altar until the opening reaches the surface of the earth.
This shall cause all untimely [calamities] to cease.
Calamities such as torrential rain, thunder, hail, and lightning shall all cease at once.
Furthermore, Venerable Ānanda, there is a mantra that pacifies all calamities,
obstacles, hot winds, cold winds, whirlwinds, and malignant winds.
It can protect all crops, flowers, fruits, and their flavors.
The mantra for quelling winds in the eastern direction is:
*Tadyathā | hula hula | mandabrumayaneśi | nṛṣṭajita | mihicakreṇa | nagna* (or *nagana*).
1. Gavadaṃ, 2. Meghavaṃ, 3. Varṣavaṃ, 4. Mitravaṃ, 5. Garajavaṃ, 6.
Aśanivaṃ, 7. Siyambalavaṃ, 8. Sañjambhavaṃ, 9. Svāhā.
This is the *huṃ*-mantra for pacifying the winds of the southern direction.
1. Ruhu ru | 2. Manda-nokṣiṇa-jvālini | 3. Nṛtyati-citta | 4. Mikheda-khaṅga | 5.

Venerable Ānanda, you should perform these mantras of the four directions using the aforementioned ritual procedure.
This shall cause all calamities, obstacles, and evil winds that destroy the sprouts and seedlings to be entirely stilled.
Furthermore, Āyuṣmat Ānanda, there is another mantra capable of stilling all the poisonous breath of malevolent nāgas,
as well as sudden winds, thunder, hail, and torrential rains that destroy the sprouts and seedlings.
The mantra for quelling sudden wind, thunder, hail, and torrential rain is as follows:

*Ṭa ṭa ra ṭa ra (1) *cili cili (2) *vara vara vara (3) *mili mili (4) *ja ja ja ja (5) *tiṣṭha saṃluḍa duṣṭān (6) svāhā (7). The mantra for subduing poisonous nāgas: *dudu dudu (1) mahā-dudulaye (2) svāhā (3) *ru ru luḍaduṣṭān bhakṣaya nāgān (4) *sarvataḥ samīkṣya (5) *savalisa (6) *samitsu śakrājña (7) *sa āśrava (8) *sase suṅga (9) *vala-bhagna (10) *sanāga-janma (11) svāhā (12). If the Venerable Ānanda wishes to practice these mantras and their samayas, [he should do so].
First, before the images of the Buddhas of the ten directions,
one should use various scented waters to smear and decorate a circular maṇḍala measuring two cubits in diameter.
Furthermore, at a clean spot along the path,
smear a two-cubit square maṇḍala with pure substances;
then take a brand-new, clean one-dǒu jar.
Fill [a vessel] with pure water and place it upon the altar before the Buddha;
one should make offerings of seasonal incense and flowers,
using only aloeswood, white sandalwood, frankincense, and the like.
Having made offerings by burning and boiling [the substances],
one should hold a willow branch in the hand and place it within the water jar,
reciting this mantra aloud and with rapid cadence.
It gathers all venomous dragons, evil winds, torrential rains, calamities, and poisonous vapors, causing them to enter entirely into the water jar and restraining them there.
By reciting the mantra twenty-one times over the water jar, one restrains and strictly controls it; thus one holds this water jar.
The opening at the top of the earthen altar is closed with soil.
One waits until the wind and rain have ceased and it is calm, pure, and clear;
only then does one remove the jar.
Venerable Ānanda, there is also a mantra of Kāśyapa:

*Namo buddhāya | namo dharmāya | namaḥ saṃghāya | tadyathā | oṃ | hāra hāra hāra hāra | ha ha ha ha ha ha ha | namo kaśyapāya | tathāgatāya | arhate samyaksaṃbuddhāya | siddhyantu mantrapadāni svāhā.* The Buddha said to Ānanda: "If there are any evil nāgas..."
When heavy rain has fallen for a long time and the weather remains unsettled, one should cleanse the ground of the path and the site where the homa is to be performed.
At that time, one should gather one hundred and eighty flowers of various exquisite fragrances.
He took them to offer to the Buddha.
Having finished offering them to the Buddha,
he then sat down cross-legged upon the ground along that path, facing west.
Reciting the mantra with a loud voice and rapid cadence, consecrate one flower at a time and use it for homa;
once these flowers are exhausted, all obstacles such as the poisonous breath of evil nāgas, calamities, torrential rains, and fierce winds will be eliminated.
At that time, the weather cleared and settled;
it eliminated the calamities of famine for all sentient beings and protected and benefited all crops, flowers, fruits, and seeds.
The flavors shall be fully prepared and perfected.
If the weather does not clear, perform the ritual twice as many times as before, according to the Dharma,
offering once, twice, or even up to five times.
The weather will certainly clear.
The mantra-practitioner shall bathe to cleanse the body and clothing,
and refrain from all speech and discourse.
Through the great mind of loving-kindness, one achieves accomplishment by governing the Dharma according to the Dharma.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Furthermore, there is a mantra whose power can ward off all evil dragons, malevolent insects, and beasts that devour seedlings."
It can also dispel all ghosts and spirits that suck the vital essence from humans,
causing them all to flee and scatter;
it can bestow [benefits] upon all sentient beings in the world.
It brings about great peace and happiness;
crops and fruits will always flourish and attain great abundance.
This is the root mantra for extinguishing all calamities.

At that time, when the Tathāgata spoke this mantra, [the earth shook in six ways].
In all the world, fires break out within the palaces of all the evil,
venomous nāgas. These venomous nāgas, scorched by the fire, all suffer from headaches,
and their bodies and skin are completely scorched and ruined.
Their limbs were in pain and they were all simultaneously filled with terror.
They went before the Buddha, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet,
and with palms joined in reverence, they spoke in unison.
He addressed the World-Honored One, saying: "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata now speaks this mantra, causing all the nāgas to experience extreme fear and distress.
World-Honored One, we nāgas have committed no transgression."
Those who constantly practice the dharma of holding evil mantras always harass and disturb us nāgas and our like—whether by binding, beating, imprisoning, or chasing us away.
They cause us and our retinues to leave our own palaces; because of this, we all give rise to great wrath.
Consequently, untimely great and violent winds, sudden and fierce rains, thunder, hail, and lightning bolts were sent forth.
By these causes of suffering, O World-Honored One, all crops, flowers, fruits,
and the flavors of their produce were ruined and destroyed.
May all [sufferings] be diminished.
Therefore, O World-Honored One, those who uphold the mantra should always [direct their compassion] toward all sentient beings within the six realms of existence.
He gave rise to a mind of great compassion for the benefit and happiness [of beings].
By the power of this arising of great compassion,
the World-Honored One caused all calamities, pestilences, poisons, evil winds, and evil rains to be completely extinguished.
"Blessed One, we nāgas and others now each make a vow before the Buddha:
wherever this mantra is present and whoever upholds it,"
Furthermore, it shall not damage any crops, flowers, fruits, or seeds.
If there is one who can constantly transcribe such mantras according to the Dharma,
receive and uphold them, recite them, and perform the ritual boundary-binding (sīmābandha) in accordance with the rules.
To protect all crops, flowers, fruits, and flavors,
we, the various classes of nāgas,
shall go among them and provide protection for all.
May the winds and rains be timely, so that all crops, flowers, fruits,
and seeds shall be endowed with full flavor and sweetness;
may all untimely, evil winds, torrential rains, thunder, hail, and lightning never again occur.
It can cause calamities such as frost, mist, and poisonous vapors,
and it is also able to ward off all enemies, thieves, malevolent spirits, ghosts, and various kinds of insects and beasts.
We shall not allow any harm or violence to be inflicted upon any sentient beings, nor upon any crops, flowers, fruits,
or seeds. We, the various classes of nāgas,
will each exhort one another not to cause destruction or bring about any calamities.
At that time, the Tathāgata addressed the nāgas, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, you nāgas!
You should thus provide various forms of protection for all sentient beings within the realm of Jambudvīpa."
They shall attain great peace and happiness.
At that time, the Tathāgata again addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"In this way, during the final age at the end of the times, [this mantra shall prevail]."
It is capable of providing protection for all crops, flowers, fruits, and flavors;
furthermore, it can dispel all pestilential poisons, diseases, calamities, and disasters.
Should there be malevolent dragons that repeatedly give rise to calamitous vapors, evil winds, thunder, hail, and torrential rains—
At that time, one should proceed to the summit of a high mountain or go to a field and construct a square maṇḍala measuring four cubits,
using scented water, yellow earth, and *gomaya*.
It was adorned and decorated according to the Dharma,
with the boundaries of the city walls clearly demarcated and its four gates opened wide.
Using saffron paste,
one should draw eight-petaled blossoming lotus flowers on the four sides, the four corners, and the center.
Using rice flour paste dyed in five colors,
the boundary lines were smoothed and decorated,
and the four gates were adorned with colorful patterns.
Take red calf-dung and fresh cow dung,
mix them with white flour to form a dough,
and fashion the bodies of the five dragon kings according to the ritual rules.
Facing the east of the altar is the Three-Headed Dragon King;
from atop his heads emerge three snake-dragon heads.
On the south side is the Five-Headed Dragon King;
from atop his heads emerge five snake-dragon heads.
On the west side is the Seven-Headed Dragon King.
From the heads emerge seven snake-heads;
facing north is the Nine-Headed Dragon King,
from whose heads emerge nine snake-heads.
In the center is a dragon king;
from his head emerges the head of a snake-headed dragon.
The body size of these dragon kings is twelve finger-widths.
Their facial features and physical forms resemble those of celestial deities;
all are seated in the half-lotus posture upon eight-petaled lotuses,
adorned with various garments in accordance with the Dharma.
Place jars of fragrant water at each of the four gates and four corners.
In front of each dragon, place an incense burner and a tray of the seven kinds of food and the three white foods.
Place clean ceramic jars filled with milk, curd, and butter,
as well as jars filled with powdered non-glutinous rice,
before the five dragon kings.
Arrange the offerings according to the Dharma,
scattering various seasonal flowers as an offering,
and burning aloeswood incense and storax to present as an offering.
Consecrate the rice grains, white mustard seeds,
and the five types of vajra-kīlas scattered upon the altar;
four of these are made of khadira wood.
A piece of *tāla* wood,
or one made of tempered steel,
measuring four finger-widths in length.
Thus, empower the five stakes with the mantra one hundred and eight times.
Drive the vajra-wood stakes into the four directions at the *nāga-citā*,
and drive the vajra-iron stake into the center at the *nāga-citā*.
At each of the four corners of the altar, erect a banner-pole sixteen cubits long; write this mantra upon plain silk cloths and tie them to the tops of the four banners.
Recite this mantra twenty-one times.
Having empowered the four banners, he erected them;
with a fearful countenance and a startled mind,
he gazed toward the ten directions and recited this mantra thirty-five times in a loud, rapid, and clear voice.
Wherever the eye reaches shall constitute the boundary.
May it protect and bless all fields, groves, gardens, and all crops, flowers, fruits, and seeds throughout the ten directions,
until the removal of the altar’s banner.
They shall always obtain protection for all their crops, flowers, fruits, and seeds,
such that they are not harmed by any locusts, various malevolent birds and beasts, fierce winds, torrential rains, lightning, thunderbolts, or any evil venomous dragons.
Yet they cause calamities, ruin, and injury;
[now, however,] may all the five grains, sprouts, crops, flowers, fruits, and seeds within that kingdom become entirely abundant and ripe.
All the dragon kings will provide protection.
Furthermore, empower clean sand one hundred and eight times with the mantra and scatter it everywhere throughout the fields and gardens, upon all the crops, flowers, fruits, and trees.
By this empowerment, they shall likewise not cause calamity for all locusts, bipeds, multi-peds,
or various insects and beasts that greedily devour the sprouts, flowers, fruits, and seeds of the crops.
Furthermore, one should prepare a square altar within a field or a garden according to its dimensions,
duly smearing and purifying it with *homa* offerings. Then,
take wood from the *kṣīravṛkṣa* (milk-tree) or the *khadira* tree.
Take two handfuls of straight-ended stalks and cut them;
empower them and ignite the fire.
One should use barley, sesame, non-glutinous rice, white mustard seeds, and clarified butter.
Recite the mantra three times each day;
empower one [substance] and burn it one hundred and eight times.
Continue in this manner without interruption for a full seven days.
Then all the evil nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas,
and various malevolent spirits who roam the world and bring about calamities will be driven away and utterly dispersed.
Furthermore, all locusts, birds, beasts,
and other creatures that devour people's seedlings, crops, flowers, fruits,
and seeds shall likewise be entirely eliminated.
Furthermore, according to another method, during the second and third months of spring,
or the seventh and eighth months of autumn,
one should go to the summit of a high mountain or to a high and commanding vantage point within a field.
Or, on the upper floor of a tower facing the heavens,
one should remain pure according to the Dharma for seven days and seven nights,
and then adorn an eight-cubit maṇḍala.
On each of the four sides, erect a separate banner-pole.
Atop each of the four banners,
tie and suspend a long silk pennant measuring one zhang and six chi in length.
On the inner surface of each banner,
paint an image of Śākyamuni Tathāgata;
to the right of the Buddha, paint the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi Guhyapati.
On the left, paint the Ṛṣi Agasti with his banner-palm pointing downward; here,
transcribe the text of this mantra-sūtra.
Four kīlas made of red sandalwood,
each three spans in length;
empower them with the mantra twenty-one times.
Drive four stakes below [the center] to mark and bind the square boundary. Then,
offer seasonal varieties of exquisite flowers, incense, food, drink, fruits, and nuts.
Having spread out the offerings,
one should observe the crops in the fields throughout the ten directions during the hours of the tiger (寅), rabbit (卯), dragon (辰),
snake (巳), horse (午), sheep (未), monkey (申), rooster (酉), and pig (亥).

Burn incense and invoke all Buddhas of the ten directions, all great Bodhisattvas, and all celestial beings, sages, dragons, spirits, and the eight classes of supernatural beings to descend and bestow their protection.
Recite this mantra one hundred and eight times.
If one practices this purification for a full seven days and nights,
one will then be able to eliminate all calamities and obstacles such as malignant winds, torrential rains, thunder, and hail. Furthermore,
one will be able to eliminate two-legged, four-legged, and many-legged creatures, including locusts, birds, and beasts.
Those who were devouring the crops, flowers, fruits,
and seeds all fled and dispersed. Furthermore,
all dangers from venomous snakes, tigers, wolves, and the like were eliminated, and all calamities and obstacles were entirely extinguished.
The Venerable Ānanda, there is also the root heart-mantra:
Namo buddhāya | oṃ hiri miri | caṇi mi ri li | caṇi caṇi mantāye | svāhā || The Buddha said to Ānanda: "This is the heart-mantra."
If there is anyone who can believe, understand, accept, and uphold this at the summit of a high mountain,
and empower a pomegranate staff with this mantra one thousand and eighty times;
Holding a staff in his right hand and forming the Dragon-Sitting Mudrā with his left,
he gazes upon heaven and earth in the ten directions.
Regarding crops in the fields,
if one recites the mantra once with a roar of wrathful anger and brandishes a staff as if to strike,
the [pests] will be expectedly halted and warded off.
If one recites it separately one thousand and eighty times,
all evil and venomous dragons and the like will have the hair on their bodies bristle with terror and remain restless with fear.
The poisonous mind is extinguished,
and all evil winds, evil rains, poisonous vapors, thunder, hail, and lightning are immediately ceased and eliminated.
Furthermore, according to another method, on the first and eighth days of the third month:
In a spacious and elevated location within that wilderness,
one should prepare the ground with purity and construct a four-cubit maṇḍala,
beautifully adorned with scented water, yellow earth, and *gomaya*.
The ground is thoroughly coated with white sandalwood incense paste.
The boundary lines are marked out, the four gates are opened wide, and eight stakes of red sandalwood and vajra are consecrated twenty-one times simultaneously.
Drive stakes into the four corners and the four gates to establish the boundary.
Consecrate five new arrows seven times.
Insert iron tridents with three prongs made of tempered steel at the four corners.
Place them upright at the center of the altar.
Empower five-colored cords by reciting the mantra seven times.
It is surrounded on all four sides by a boundary.
At the center of the four corners, place argha water consisting of white sandalwood, saffron, and water.
Insert various flowering branches and leaves into the mouth of the jar.
At the center of each of the four gates, place five incense burners and various kinds of "three-white" foods and drinks;
these should be arranged and offered at the centers of the four gates according to the ritual rules.
Furthermore, at that time, various incenses and flowers were scattered about,
and agallochum, storax, aloeswood, white sandalwood, and frankincense were burned as offerings.
Consecrate rice grains, white mustard seeds, and flowers according to the ritual rules and scatter them upon the altar.
Consecrate the water with white mustard seeds seven times.
He scattered [the seeds] throughout the ten directions to establish a boundary.
For seven days,
during each of the six periods of the day, he observed the fields and crops in the ten directions.
Reciting the heart-mantra with a resolute voice one thousand and eighty times for seven days and nights,
one will then attain [the result] within eight months thereafter.
Throughout the ten directions for the distance of one yojana,
there shall be no yakṣas, rākṣasas, ghosts, spirits,
or any species of malevolent insects that devour crops, flowers, fruits, or seeds.
All shall be completely dispelled.
The mantra-holder should bathe and purify themselves, anoint the body with incense,
don clean garments, and practice according to the Dharma.
Kneel with the right knee on the ground at the western gate.
Empower the pomegranate staff by reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times.
Grasp the staff with the right hand while forming the Dragon-Sitting Seal (*nāgasana-mudrā*) with the left hand.
The left thumb is bent across within the palm;
the middle and ring fingers are bent down to press upon the thumb.
With the index finger extended straight and slightly bent,
and the little finger extended straight,
the mantra practitioner circumambulates the eight directions of the mandala.
Standing, recite the mantra seventeen times for each [deity].
Then, facing the place where the clouds and rain arise,
recite the mantra once while consecrating your staff.
Strike once to dispel the enemy's evil winds, clouds, and rain,
sending them down into great mountain valleys.
Perform this striking and dispersing one thousand and eighty times.
Those evil nāgas will then extinguish their poisonous intent,
and the wind and rain will cease.
If they do not cease, one should again apply double the previous amount of the ritual method.
All those evil nāgas suffered from headaches, heartaches, and bodily pains as hot sand clung to their bodies;
they experienced suffering as if their limbs were being cut by knives.
These evil nāgas were struck with great terror.
Ānanda, by means of this Dharma,
all the malevolent nāgas within the realm of Jambudvīpa shall abide according to the law for eight months.
It shall send down a great rain of sweet dew.
Should there be heat, cold winds, torrential rains, thunder, hail,
or lightning that repeatedly arise in disorder to cause calamities, [it shall pacify them].
